title: Touch-move: the rule that makes you commit
description: In serious chess, if you touch a piece you must move it. Touch-move sounds like etiquette; it is actually a training rule for the mind — it punishes the hover and rewards deciding before you reach.

body.heading: Touch it, move it
paragraphs: The rule is simple: a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it if a legal move exists, and a player who touches an opponent's piece must capture it if they can. The only escape is announcing 'I adjust' before touching a piece just to centre it on its square.

Casual games often waive the rule, and that is fine between friends. But playing a few games with touch-move on changes your habits within an hour: the hand stops wandering over the board auditioning moves.

body.heading: Decide first, reach second
paragraphs: Strong players calculate with their eyes, not their fingers. Touch-move forces that discipline early — you learn to hold a move in your head, check it once more, and only then commit your hand.
Try it as a house rule for one evening and notice the second effect: games get calmer. No hovering, no take-backs, no arguments — just decisions, owned.

takeaway: Touch-move turns chess into decision training: announce 'I adjust' or commit — calculate with your eyes first and let your hand move only once.
